title: Re:Cognize - A Framework For Open-Set Comic Character Re-Identification
claim: Closed-set matching against a prebuilt gallery fails on unseen entities; ours streams queries and builds the gallery as the story unfolds.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right with arrows, example then closed-set then ours
description: Three columns connected by grey arrows. The left column, titled "a reader's question: who appears where", shows a blue rounded box with the question "where Takagi asks Mashiro" above a 2x2 grid of manga page crops with two characters outlined in blue and orange. The middle column, "closed-set Re-ID", shows a grey box labelled "fixed gallery, built in advance" holding three face crops. Two query crops sit below, with arrows pointing up to the gallery and an orange "no match" label. The right column, in blue "RE:COGNIZE", shows four protocol chips: P1 full and P2 seeded in blue, P3 empty and P4 grows in orange. Below them is a query stream q1, q2, q3, ... and a blue box reading "VOUCH: grow only where additions beat the gallery they join". Captions sit under each column. Grey headers contrast with the blue title for the proposed method.
caption: Recognising characters while the story is read. On the left, a reader's question such as where Takagi asks Mashiro depends on who appears on which page. In the centre, standard Re-ID matches each query against a gallery built before reading starts, so a new character finds no match. On the right, \Recog streams crops in reading order against four galleries that hold every character (P1), a few labelled examples of each (P2), none (P3) or a few that grow as it reads (P4), and \Vouch grows the gallery only where the page vouches for a crop.
abstract: Comics and manga tell stories through characters whose appearances change from panel to panel, yet readers recognise them hundreds of pages later without ever consulting a cast list. Character re-identification models rarely face the same challenge: existing evaluations give them a fixed set of identities before the story begins. \textbf{Re:Cognize} instead asks models to recognise characters as the story unfolds and learn who is who along the way. Across three manga corpora, we evaluate five Re-ID backbones and \textbf{MECHA}, a memory-augmented baseline we introduce, and find that the central difficulty lies somewhere unexpected. Recognising familiar characters is nearly solved. Knowing which matches to trust is not. When models build a gallery and grow it from their own predictions, their performance deteriorates, even though correct identity labels would improve it by over twenty points. This raises a simple question: when should a model trust its own match? We derive a single comparison that determines when gallery updates improve recognition and use it to design \textbf{VOUCH}, which updates its memory only when the page provides supporting evidence. Without fitting additional parameters, VOUCH recovers between one-third and two-thirds of the improvement available from perfect labels. RE:COGNIZE measures whether a model can recognise characters as it reads; VOUCH shows how to remember them reliably. We focus our methodological claims on identity maintenance for previously encountered characters, while separately evaluating new-character emergence as a diagnostic under a fixed reference rule to distinguish recognition from discovery.
